title: Fleming confirms penicillin, 1928 — the mould on the dish
sources: Wikipedia: Alexander Fleming — St Mary's Hospital, London; returned 3 September 1928 from a family holiday in Suffolk; had left staphylococci culture plates on a bench; one contaminated with a fungus, colonies around it destroyed; famously remarked "That's funny"; called it "mould juice", named penicillin 7 March 1929; penicillin languished largely forgotten in the 1930s, no one believed him; praised Florey and Chain for transforming the laboratory curiosity into a practical drug; by D-Day in 1944 enough penicillin to treat all the wounded of the Allied troops; shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Florey and Chain; described as the first antibiotic substance discovered; quote "One sometimes finds what one is not looking for"

Wikipedia: Penicillin — observed by chance on 3 September 1928 that fungal contamination of a Staphylococcus aureus culture appeared to kill the bacteria; confirmed this observation with a new experiment on 28 September 1928

Wikipedia: History of penicillin — summer break with family in Suffolk; plates left on a corner of the table; on return found one with an open lid, contaminated with a blue-green mould; bacteria around the mould did not grow; concluded the mould was releasing a substance that inhibited bacterial growth
Wikipedia: Howard Florey — Oxford, Sir William Dunn School of Pathology; shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Fleming and Chain

post.facebook:
On this day in 1928, Alexander Fleming confirmed the accident behind the first antibiotic.

That summer, before a family holiday, he left dishes of bacteria on a bench in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital in London. When he came back on 3 September, one dish had been contaminated by a blue-green mould — and around it, the bacteria had been destroyed. "That's funny," he said.

On 28 September a new experiment confirmed it: the mould was releasing something that killed bacteria. For months he called it "mould juice". Then he named it penicillin.

For years almost nobody cared. It took Howard Florey and Ernst Chain in Oxford to turn it into a medicine — and by D-Day in 1944 there was enough to treat all the wounded Allied troops. In 1945 the three men shared the Nobel Prize.

Fleming put it simply: "One sometimes finds what one is not looking for."
